topic.subject: science
topic.title: Soil
topic.scope: soil profile and horizons, types of soil, percolation, water retention, soil and crops, soil erosion

misconceptions.statement: Soil is just small pieces of rock and nothing else.
misconceptions.why: Students only see the mineral component and ignore the microscopic organic matter.
misconceptions.fix: Soil is a mixture of rock particles and humus, which is organic matter from dead organisms.

probe.question: If you grind a clean rock into powder, is it now soil?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because soil is just powdered rock.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Soil forms very quickly, like after a heavy rainstorm.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the movement of soil with the creation of soil.
misconceptions.fix: Soil formation is a very slow process that takes hundreds or thousands of years to form just a few centimeters.

probe.question: How long does it take for a new layer of soil to form from rock?
probe.wrong_answer: A few days or weeks after it rains.

misconceptions.root_belief: geological changes happen on human timescales

misconceptions.statement: The deeper you dig, the more fertile the soil becomes.
misconceptions.why: Students often think 'more' material or 'older' material means more nutrients.
misconceptions.fix: The topsoil (A-horizon) is the most fertile layer because it contains the most humus.

probe.question: Which layer of soil is best for plant growth?
probe.wrong_answer: The deepest layers near the bedrock.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Soil is a solid mass and does not contain any air.
misconceptions.why: Soil looks like a continuous solid to the naked eye.
misconceptions.fix: Soil contains small spaces between its particles which are filled with air and water.

probe.question: Why do bubbles come out when you pour water on dry soil in a glass?
probe.wrong_answer: The water is boiling or reacting chemically.

misconceptions.root_belief: solids are completely solid without gaps

misconceptions.statement: Clay particles are larger than sand particles because clay feels heavy.
misconceptions.fix: Clay particles are actually the smallest, while sand particles are the largest among the three types.

probe.question: Which soil type has the smallest particle size?

misconceptions.root_belief: sensory perception is always a direct measure

misconceptions.statement: Percolation and absorption are the exact same thing.
misconceptions.why: Both involve water moving into the soil.
misconceptions.fix: Percolation is the downward movement of water through soil layers, while absorption is the soil soaking up and holding the water.

probe.question: If water passes through soil very quickly, does it have high absorption?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it took in the water quickly.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Sandy soil is the best for holding water for plants.
misconceptions.why: Students see water disappear into sand and think it is being 'stored'.
misconceptions.fix: Sandy soil has large spaces that let water drain away quickly; clayey soil holds the most water.

probe.question: Which soil would stay wet the longest after a rain?

misconceptions.statement: Any crop can grow in any soil if you just add enough water.
misconceptions.why: Students overemphasize water as the only requirement for plants.
misconceptions.fix: Different crops need different soil types; for example, wheat needs clayey-loam while cotton needs sandy-loam.

probe.question: Can we grow paddy (rice) in sandy soil if we water it every day?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because plants only need water to grow.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Soil erosion only happens in places where there are no people.
misconceptions.why: Students associate erosion with 'wild' nature or deserts only.
misconceptions.fix: Erosion happens everywhere, and human activities like deforestation and overgrazing actually speed it up.

probe.question: Does cutting down trees in a city affect soil erosion?
probe.wrong_answer: No, erosion only happens in the desert or mountains.

misconceptions.root_belief: nature and humans are separate systems

misconceptions.statement: Plants cause soil erosion because their roots break the rocks into soil.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the process of weathering with the process of erosion.
misconceptions.fix: While roots help in weathering, plants are the best way to prevent erosion because roots bind the soil particles together.

probe.question: How do trees affect the topsoil during a flood?
probe.wrong_answer: They make it easier for soil to wash away by loosening it.

misconceptions.statement: A higher percolation rate means the soil is better at soaking up water.
misconceptions.why: Students think 'higher rate' always means 'better' or 'more'.
misconceptions.fix: A higher percolation rate means water passes through faster and is NOT soaked up; sandy soil has the highest rate.

probe.question: If Soil A has a percolation rate of 50ml/min and Soil B has 10ml/min, which holds more water?
probe.wrong_answer: Soil A, because its rate is higher.

misconceptions.root_belief: faster or more is always better

misconceptions.statement: The C-horizon is made of soft mud because it is underground.
misconceptions.why: Students assume everything underground is wet and soft.
misconceptions.fix: The C-horizon consists of small lumps of rocks with cracks and is quite hard compared to topsoil.

probe.question: Is it easier to dig through the A-horizon or the C-horizon?
probe.wrong_answer: The C-horizon because it is moist and soft.
